About Me
I am a Wesleyan University senior investigating how data and communication, as interwoven practices, influence public life. My work focuses on crafting experiments and designing narratives that make evidence accessible and encourage civic engagement.

Data & Research: Conducting surveys and assessing behavioral data to test hypotheses and inform strategy
Communication & Writing: Transforming complex research and realities into engaging narratives for public and professional audiences.
Versatile Application: Navigating interdisciplinary contexts to provide clear insights: from courses, to corporations, to clients.

title: University Major Portfolio
text:
During the fall of my junior year, I pitched and was approved for a self-designed University Major in Data & Communication.
The major considers data and rhetoric as two languages of evidence that together influence how contemporary societies understand truth, establish credibility, and motivate collective action. It aims to study communication empirically, examine the communication of data ethically, and to explore how these modes of evidence operate in tandem and shape our perspectives on data, rhetoric, and the social world.
As part of my assessment for this major, I have developed a portfolio exploring a range of genres and audiences. The following artifacts span everything from survey design to statistical modeling to presentation development to persuasive writing. The goal is to practice writing modes from all three pillars of the major: Data Analysis and Research Methodology, Rhetorical Theory and Writing Praxis, and the Social Psychology of Civic Engagement; and reflect on these interdisciplinary approaches.

title: An Op-ed on Tempered Radicalism
text: The op-ed, “Tired of Choosing Between Selling Out and Shouting?”, championed tempered radicalism as a pathway for those working inside institutions to create meaningful change through collaboration, coalition building, and showing up for others. Grounded in social psychology research, it made the argument that in our polarized society, we need not only activists, but also committed, imaginative insiders to take action.

title: An Op-ed on Tempered Radicalism
text: The op-ed, “Tired of Choosing Between Selling Out and Shouting?”, championed tempered radicalism as a pathway for those working inside institutions to create meaningful change through collaboration, coalition building, and showing up for others. Grounded in social psychology research, it made the argument that in our polarized society, we need not only activists, but also committed, imaginative insiders to take action.

title: An Op-ed on Tempered Radicalism
text:
Context & Constraints
I first heard about tempered radicalism in Erskine and Bilimoria’s 2019 journal article White Allyship of Afro-Diasporic Women in the Workplace: A Transformative Strategy for Organizational Change. At the time I was navigating a changing sense of identity as a worker, and took a prominent interest in any and all conceptualizations of changemakers. Tempered Radicals stood out to me as they were distinct from the constrictive narratives of work I was familiar with: corporate sell-outs, burnt-out activists, broke NGO employees. Tempered radicalism reflected a lot of long-standing beliefs I held but hadn’t yet seen represented in the workplace.
I decided to focus on them for my Seminar on Social Action course final. For this project, we were tasked with presenting a clear position on a social, educational, or cultural issue and grounding our arguments in social psychology research. Furthermore, our articles had to be 800 words or less, requiring precision and concision, both of which were initially outside my comfort zone.

title: An Op-ed on Tempered Radicalism
text:
Approach
As part of the course structure, we wrote outlines, provided first drafts, completed peer reviews during a workshop led by a university writing tutor, and then submitted final drafts. To collect sources, I primarily used my university library portal to find articles under the keyword “tempered radical”, then expanding to terms I needed to define like “constructive deviance” or fields I wanted to find explorations within, “tempered radicals manufacturing.”
As I wrote my first draft, I converted my readings to audios using Paper2Audio and listened to them while doing chores or going on walks. This allowed me to read many more sources during the busiest part of the semester and to assess which sources were worth using, or rereading, and which could be set aside.
For my final draft, I used the feedback I had received encouraging me to add more examples, limit hedging language, and employ a decisive tone to appeal to the genre norms. I also read and analyzed many op-ed and tried to apply their techniques: clear language, direct appeals, and more repetition than I might typically use.

title: An Op-ed on Tempered Radicalism
text:
What I Learned
As difficult as it was to experiment with a new format, to conduct a deep dive into research surrounding institutional change, to finish my revisions before the short deadline; the real challenge of this project was not in its writing, but in its publishing.
I decided in January that 2026 would be a year of publishing, of giving my imperfect writing and beliefs to the public for all to see. This was a terrifying proposition. I struggle with perfectionism, I hate making mistakes, and I worry far too much about what people will think of me. I found this was getting in the way of my ability to grow as a writer and thinker, as I was avoiding opportunities to write. So on April 24th, I published this article to the Wesleyan Argus. And when I didn’t die, I decided to make a Substack.

title: An Op-ed on Tempered Radicalism
text:
So What?
I don’t agree with the entirety of this article anymore. In the space between its writing and now, I’ve read more than 40 books on social theory and political history, and reimaginings of our future. I studied abroad in Germany, connected with family in London, and spent a lot of time at train stations and bus stops thinking. I’ve come to see tempered radicals as a small part of a wide group of builders and would write a somewhat different article if I was starting this project from scratch. I would emphasize the need for collective pursuits inside the workplace, the importance of community-building outside of the office to create security, and the challenge and discomfort that comes with being a builder.
Notably, though, I still agree with its core messages: we can all be a part of building a better world regardless of our job title, we need to form broader coalitions and make allies even within corporate spaces, we must understand our institutions and work for more than just our own survival.
Furthermore, audience-based communication is a core tenet of my Data & Communication major, so this article isn’t worthless. It wouldn’t be even if I one day disagreed with every single word. It’s a learning opportunity. And given that the world didn’t end just because my opinions have evolved, I guess I’ll have to keep writing. Ultimately, writing helps us sharpen our thinking. As a worldbuilder, I consider it a paramount skill.

title: Statistical Consulting Project: Community Health Services
text: In Fall 2025, I worked as part of a three-person team to provide statistical consulting and data analysis for a community-based health organization in New England. We examined how demographic, behavioral, and clinical characteristics predicted adverse health events in order to help the organization understand their patients and target resources effectively. To this end, we engaged in conversations with the client regularly, and provided iterative analyses, an oral presentation, a final report, and reproducible R code.

title: Statistical Consulting Project: Community Health Services
text: In Fall 2025, I worked as part of a three-person team to provide statistical consulting and data analysis for a community-based health organization in New England. We examined how demographic, behavioral, and clinical characteristics predicted adverse health events in order to help the organization understand their patients and target resources effectively. To this end, we engaged in conversations with the client regularly, and provided iterative analyses, an oral presentation, a final report, and reproducible R code.

title: Statistical Consulting Project: Community Health Services
text:
Context & Constraints
As part of Wesleyan University’s Statistical Consulting course, two other students and myself were paired together based on our distribution of skills and assigned to an organization’s research project. As these projects involved working with depersonalized, sensitive data and getting behind the scenes of the organization, we all signed NDAs and maintain confidentiality about the project. To this end, we used private drives and github repositories, and took strict measures to ensure the data was not externally shared.
The data we worked with included patient health forms and it had not been cleaned. As a team, we navigated incomplete records and lack of documentation. We also maintained high ethical standards and transparency throughout the process, completing the CITI human subjects training, providing documentation throughout the process, and adhering to scientific standards of integrity.

title: Statistical Consulting Project: Community Health Services
text:
Approach
For this project, we conducted an intake interview with the client to translate goals and objectives into measurable research hypotheses. We cleaned the data, completed a short literature review, and determined our approach to answering these questions: descriptive statistics, multinomial logit regressions, and a latent class analysis. Team code was shared and managed using Git/Github to allow for reproducibility, version control, and collaboration.

title: Statistical Consulting Project: Community Health Services
text:
What I Learned
In this course, we not only learned to use Github and new methods of analysis, but also spent a lot of time exploring the nonstatistical aspects of statistical consulting. We covered ethics in data science, data storytelling, techniques for interviewing clients, and consulting reports as a writing genre. We were able to practice working directly with clients with limited familiarity with research and data analysis, using AI as a learning tool without compromising confidentiality, and completing statistical consulting projects collaboratively.
One key learning I was able to gain through this team work was the importance of cross-functional collaboration. Our team used a highly-structured division of labor. While this, improved specialization and allowed me to take ownership of our latent class analysis, it also meant that cross-review was deprioritized, and led to an error in how adverse events were measured in one section being caught later than necessary. In the future, when doing work in small teams, I would also prioritize collective ownership to strengthen cross-review and flexibility.

title: Statistical Consulting Project: Community Health Services
text:
So What?
This experience gave me the opportunity to use data analysis as more than just a tool of discovery. In working with real-world data and clients, I understand research as an act of stewardship. It taught me to work collaboratively and responsibly to navigate ambiguity and translate complex statistics into actionable insights that our client could use to continue and improve their meaningful work. Behind every data point is a person and by providing analyses through effective and ethical communication, we can honor complexity and create stronger institutions that they benefit from. This is a core tenet of my Data & Communication major: that rigorous evidence only matters if it is communicated with integrity, clarity, and empathy.

title: An Experimental Test of Change Talk Exposure in Civic Contexts
text:
Motivational Interviewing (MI) is a therapeutic technique often successfully applied in medical contexts to encourage patients to engage in pro-health behaviors, such as vaccinating children or quitting narcotics.
For this project, I wanted to see if one aspect of MI, the cultivation of change talk, could be used to affect participants’ civic engagement, adding to the growing body of interdisciplinary research seeking to drive people towards actions that make the world a better place by drawing on political theory, sociology, and psychology.
I decided to design an experiment using a Qualtrics survey to determine if viewing change talk, and its inverse, sustain talk would affect participants beliefs and intentions to engage in two forms of everyday activism, signing petitions and making small donations.
My statistical modeling in R did not provide significant results, indicating that that brief exposures to change talk may not be sufficient to shift intentions, but also that exposure to sustain talk may not be able to do the same.
To share these findings, I wrote a research paper, delivered a presentation, and devised a poster, all linked below.

title: An Experimental Test of Change Talk Exposure in Civic Contexts
text:
Context & Constraints
This project grew from a desire to bridge related interests of mine: psychology, communication, and persuasion, through research seeking to drive civic engagement. In my reading, I stumbled upon MI and learned that there was a growing body of literature successfully applying its tactics to new contexts, including business leadership, physicians’ continued education, and limited civic engagement research. However, while MI has seen wide success as an intervention, it’s also a complex therapeutic technique.
Due to concerns about the feasibility of a project employing MI in full: lack access to paid trainings, unlikely IRB approval for such interventions, and the small sample size an interview-based intervention would garner; change talk—a core element MI associated with sustained, positive behavioral change—was assessed instead. The simple principles of change and sustain talk made it possible to develop a straightforward experiment and a fast, easy to complete survey that could host more questions and obtain more participants.

title: An Experimental Test of Change Talk Exposure in Civic Contexts
text:
Approach
For this study, I decided to compare the impact of change talk and sustain talk on civic engagement in two distinct forms of everyday collective action to assess whether my results were domain specific. I selected petition signing and small donations as they would be familiar to the most convenient and sizable population available: college students, while lacking the social pressure of domains like recycling and voting.
From these domains and talk types, I was able to design a 4-level completely randomized design, using Qualtrics to assign each respondent to read a vignette discussing either petition signing or small donations, and a student’s decision to either change their habits of not engaging or sustain their current behavior. This random assignment helped ensure that results could be attributed to the experiment rather than any placement biases.
I then used several Likert scales to develop composite scores, averaging 3 questions each: Petition-Intentions, Petition-Beliefs, Donation-Intentions, and Donation-Beliefs. I wanted to measure Intentions and Beliefs as I felt that the distinction between intending to do something and believing in the efficacy and viability of your action are distinct outcomes that don’t always overlap (e.g. you can believe that recycling isn’t helpful and still recycle because everyone you know does). I wanted to know which of these axes might be affected by exposure to change and sustain talk.
I used AI to design the messaging and layout of a promotional poster, testing several options for tone, visibility, and ease. The flyers were hung across campus, ensuring that the sample wouldn’t simply reflect the groups I associated with. I also provided a 3-winner lottery of $10 gift cards, in line with research suggesting that smaller rewards participants were more likely to receive had the stronger impact. In total, I received 120 responses.
I used the R package ordinal to conduct several ordinal analyses of variance (ANOVA), accounting for the use of Likert scales, and analyses of covariance (ANCOVA) to control for baseline civic engagement. While mean petition intention scores were higher for the petition-change talk groups, means were often variable, and I found no significant relationships between my explanatory and response variables. I tested my assumptions and used boxplots to make it easy to interpret the means, relationships, and variability of the data.




Project Image

title: An Experimental Test of Change Talk Exposure in Civic Contexts
text:
What I Learned
As this was a class final, format was largely predetermined, a research paper and a presentation. However, I was later asked to convert the project into a poster for an event where prospective university students could learn about our department.
While the paper remains a necessity for providing the greatest wealth of information and clarity surrounding my project, I found that the poster gave me a stronger understanding of my work due to its brevity and the ability to view several aspects simultaneously. I plan to turn more projects into posters, as they give me an easy, effective way to reconsider my research projects and share them with others.
This experiment also taught me a lot about study design. In my results, I found that there were a lot of incomplete surveys, especially in later sections, as well as some surveys that, while complete, failed the attention check. There is an array of factors that could explain this and three that I think warrant discussion here.
The first has to do with study length. While completable in 2-5 minutes, the survey wasn’t short. I chose to measure both intention and belief in social action. Looking back, having two response variables introduced excess complexity and, in a future case, I would study them separately and use fewer questions. I also think that in my promotion I overemphasized ease and potential monetary reward as motivations for completion. These are useful incentives, but they can undermine more intrinsic motivations, especially for longer surveys. Going forward I’d like to provide more balanced promotion.
Finally, having the attention check end of the survey made it difficult to discern if participants had read the vignettes. In the future, I would use a reading check, that prevents participants from moving forward without the correct answer.

title: An Experimental Test of Change Talk Exposure in Civic Contexts
text:
So What?
The insignificant results in this project offer an inspiring sign: while exposure to change talk does not appear to provide a substantial effect on participant behavior neither does its inverse—this means that more effortful attempts to change behavior may not be undermined by simple exposure to sustain talk.
This project contributes to a growing body of literature that seeks to help organizers inspire individuals to engage civically and contribute to wider movements. Motivational Interviewing has been successful in cultivating personal change in a range of environments and research that looks to expand its practice and principles to other fields—and to test its limits—offers a strong opportunity to learn more about this tactic and about non-manipulative persuasion tactics writ large.
